transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-12-20
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Marcus Vega (QuantumCore CTO), Lina Park (Head of Platform), Samir Patel (Security)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be imperfect): Quick intro, scope private deployment, discuss networking options (VPC peering, private endpoints), region and residency constraints, security controls. Agree to share architecture docs and run a benchmark in us-west-2.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — Alex from Redwood. How's it going?
[00:06] Marcus Vega: Hey Alex, doing good. We have Lina and Samir here, hi.
[00:09] Lina Park: Hi all.
[00:10] Samir Patel: Morning.
[00:12] Alex Chen: Great. Quick agenda: confirm QuantumCore's requirements for private / VPC deployment, networking constraints, security questions, and a pilot timeline. Priya from our infra team will cover the technical bits.
[00:20] Priya Nair: Hi — I'll jump in on the technical side, we're happy to map this to your cloud setup. Marcus, can you give high level on what you're trying to run and where?
[00:28] Marcus Vega: Sure. We're planning to embed LLM features into our analytics platform — both chat assistant and embeddings for search. Latency matters for interactive use, and we want data to stay in our account. We're leaning toward Redwood Private in our VPC, prefer us-west-2 for residency reasons.
[00:44] Priya Nair: Got it. And you're on AWS today? Any transit gateway or DX connections?
[00:49] Lina Park: Yes, primary infra in AWS. We use a transit gateway for cross-account networking and have Direct Connect to our colo. We'll likely want peering into our analytics VPC or PrivateLink.
[01:00] Alex Chen: Quick clarifying Q: is it acceptable for Redwood to connect via VPC peering, or do you require endpoint-based (PrivateLink) access?
[01:08] Samir Patel: Prefer PrivateLink if possible because it gives us more control over IPs and we can avoid spreading routes. But if peering is simpler and keeps latency lower that's worth considering.
[01:18] Priya Nair: We support both. For Private deployments we can do VPC peering, PrivateLink/Interface Endpoints, or transit gateway attachments depending on scale and CIDR constraints. Each has tradeoffs.
[01:30] Marcus Vega: What about CIDR overlap? We have a lot of legacy subnets.
[01:34] Priya Nair: If there's overlap peering won't work. In that case PrivateLink or a VPN/Direct Connect with NAT would be the fallback. We can also use a dedicated network account to avoid overlap — that's common in larger customers.
[01:46] Lina Park: Ok, can you talk through egress IPs? Our security team needs fixed egress ranges for firewall allowlists.
[01:52] Priya Nair: For VPC peering the traffic is within the AWS network so it's source-preserving; you see Redwood instance IPs in your peer ranges. For PrivateLink the interface endpoint has ENIs in your subnets — you can apply security groups. For egress to the internet from our side, you'd control NAT/GW. We can also provide a list of predictable egress IP ranges if you use our managed egress nodes in the same region.
[02:15] Samir Patel: When you say "predictable egress ranges" — are those single IPs or small ranges? We have a strict firewall policy.
[02:21] Priya Nair: Typically small CIDR blocks per deployment (like /28s or /27s). We'll include exact ranges in the infra doc.
[02:28] Alex Chen: Also note our Dedicated pools support private deployments with SLA — so if throughput is a concern we can size reserved capacity.
[02:36] Marcus Vega: Good to know. On compliance: SOC2, audit logs, SSO — we need all that.
[02:41] Alex Chen: Absolutely. We'll share SOC2 and network security docs. Priya, can you explain audit log surface for Private?
[02:47] Priya Nair: In private deployments we ship logs to your logging account via cross-account S3 or push to your SIEM via Kinesis/Firehose if you'd prefer. We support audit trails for request metadata, model version, token counts — we can persist those for your retention policy.
[03:04] Samir Patel: How do you handle keys? KMS integration? We need customer-managed keys — HSM ideally.
[03:10] Priya Nair: Yes we integrate with customer-managed KMS. For on-prem or higher security we can support HSM-backed keys. The control plane still needs to orchestrate, but encryption at rest for artifacts and model artifacts is supported with BYOK patterns.
[03:23] Marcus Vega: Great. On latency, we want sub-200ms p95 on chat. Is that realistic in us-west-2?
[03:29] Priya Nair: It depends on model family and sequence lengths. For small chat models and optimized serving, sub-200ms p95 can be achieved with co-located infra and dedicated capacity. We'll include performance baselines; we also recommend prefix-KV caching for repeated contexts.
[03:44] Lina Park: How about region failover? We have DR requirements across multiple AZs and prefer an active-passive in another region — maybe us-east-1.
[03:54] Priya Nair: We support multi-region deployments. Failover is handled via smart routing; we can set up a warm standby in us-east-1 and failover the DNS or route policy. There are replication and model sync considerations.
[04:07] Alex Chen: Quick note: some of our customers use a hybrid approach — control plane in Redwood-hosted but data plane in customer VPC. That reduces surface area and still gives isolation.
[04:17] Marcus Vega: Is that an option for us? We prefer full private deployment but open to hybrid if it lowers ops.
[04:23] Priya Nair: Yes, hybrid is an option. Full Private gives you everything in your VPC; hybrid keeps the control plane managed by Redwood but the actual inference runs in your VPC endpoints. We'll map pros/cons in the doc.
[04:34] Samir Patel: What about network latency for model downloads and kernel composition? If you're bringing models to our infra we need to know initial pull windows and caching.
[04:43] Priya Nair: Model artifacts can be pre-staged in S3 in your account or pulled from our object store. Pre-staging avoids heavy pulls during rollout. Once warmed, the runtime uses KV cache and persistent local storage so cold starts are minimised. We'll propose a staging plan.
[04:58] Alex Chen: Any regulatory constraints beyond residency? Data retention, PII handling?
[05:03] Marcus Vega: We handle PII, but we need to ensure Redwood won't persist any raw customer data outside our controls. Also retention windows are strict for logs.
[05:12] Priya Nair: For Private we can configure zero-persistence policies and retention TTLs for request logs. We support masking and field-level redaction on ingestion, but that's often a partner integration. We'll detail config knobs.
[05:25] Lina Park: Can you share a sample network diagram? Preferably with peering, PrivateLink, and transit gateway variants.
[05:31] Alex Chen: Yes — action item for Alex to share architecture diagrams and variant examples.
[05:35] [BREAK IN AUDIO] - slight overlap, transcript may skip a word
[05:42] Marcus Vega: On cost, what's the rough delta between hosted vs Dedicated vs Private?
[05:47] Priya Nair: Hosted is usually lowest friction and unit cost, Dedicated is reserved capacity with committed pricing (better unit economics at scale), and Private adds additional infra and networking overhead. We'll provide a cost anchor based on expected QPS and model choices.
[06:01] Marcus Vega: For sizing, we expect peak QPS around 120 concurrent small-chat sessions and embedding index building off-peak.
[06:10] Priya Nair: That helps. For that workload a small Dedicated pool with burst capacity should do. We'll include estimated GPU counts and instance types (A10G, H100 depending on model).
[06:22] Samir Patel: Regarding access control — SSO and RBAC — can you integrate with our SAML provider and enforce per-team access?
[06:29] Alex Chen: Yes we have SAML/SSO and fine-grained RBAC in the console for routes, models, and telemetry. For Private deployments we can connect to your IdP via SAML or OIDC, and we support SCIM for user provisioning.
[06:42] Lina Park: Does Private deployment require an extra account for Redwood infra or is it all in our account?
[06:47] Priya Nair: Typically the compute runs in customer account/VPC. The control plane may remain in Redwood-managed account unless you take the fully private on-prem package. We can also offer a customer-managed control plane — that's part of enterprise negotiation.
[07:00] Marcus Vega: How long to stand up a proof-of-concept?
[07:03] Alex Chen: From signed SOW to pilot usually 4-6 weeks — includes network setup, capacity provisioning, and a short validation benchmark. If you pre-stage models and coordinate CIDR information faster it can be quicker.
[07:15] Samir Patel: On the subject of connectivity, do you use cross-account IAM roles for S3 access when staging artifacts?
[07:21] Priya Nair: Yes cross-account roles are our preferred pattern. We provide a CloudFormation template or Terraform modules to wire up permissions and endpoints to reduce manual setup.
[07:31] Marcus Vega: About PrivateLink — do we need to open certain ports or adjust NACLs?
[07:36] Priya Nair: PrivateLink uses ENIs and typical application ports; you need to ensure security groups allow traffic from your app subnets. NACLs should permit ephemeral ports if you have strict rules. We'll provide a checklist.
[07:47] Alex Chen: Another real customer note: some companies worry about outbound logging from the control plane. We can set up all logging to go to your log buckets to satisfy that.
[07:55] Lina Park: Good. Any performance differences between peering and PrivateLink?
[07:58] Priya Nair: Peering is generally slightly lower latency because it's direct route, but only if CIDR is clean and routing is set. PrivateLink adds a hop through the interface endpoint but often negligible for most workloads. If ultra-low latency is a must, peering with colocated instances is preferred.
[08:14] Marcus Vega: What about cross-region latency if run in us-west-2 but clients are global?
[08:18] Priya Nair: We recommend routing user requests to an edge and then to the nearest region. For interactive apps global users may see higher latency; multi-region deployments reduce that. We'll show tradeoffs.
[08:30] Samir Patel: Are there any wide-known issues with transit gateways? Sometimes routing propagation gets tricky across accounts.
[08:37] Priya Nair: True — transit gateway is powerful but needs careful route table management. Our infra team can coordinate with your network engineers to set up proper route propagation and avoid accidental wide routes.
[08:48] Alex Chen: Can we pivot to operational concerns — upgrades and model rollouts?
[08:52] Priya Nair: Rollouts are handled by version pinning and canary deploys; for Private we can do canary on a subset of nodes in your VPC. We also support automatic fallback to a smaller model if there are capacity issues.
[09:03] Marcus Vega: If we need to rotate keys or change CIDRs mid-pilot, how disruptive is that?
[09:09] Priya Nair: Key rotation can be non-disruptive if done with a staged approach. CIDR changes are trickier; they often require reconfiguring peering or endpoints. We'll plan for final CIDR confirmation early.
[09:20] [15:00 MARKER MISMATCH NOTE: timestamps approximate]
[09:25] Marcus Vega: For the benchmark run, can you run a test using our sample prompt set and our data residency constraints?
[09:31] Alex Chen: Yes, we'll schedule a benchmark in us-west-2 using your prompt set. Priya will lead the run and we'll share results and logs.
[09:39] Priya Nair: We'll need your CIDR ranges, preferred subnets, and example payload sizes. Also the model families you want to test.
[09:49] Lina Park: We'll provide that by Tuesday.
[09:52] Samir Patel: One more: does Redwood support private image registries for model containers? Some of our tooling expects images in our ECR.
[09:59] Priya Nair: Yes we can bring your ECR images or stage images in your account. We also support pulling from our registry if that's simpler.
[10:08] Alex Chen: Wrapping up — recapping action items: Alex to send infra diagram and SOC2/doc links; Priya to prepare capacity estimate and deploy checklist; Samir to send CIDR ranges. We'll schedule the benchmark for next week pending your inputs.
[10:24] Marcus Vega: Sounds good. Any blockers from your side?
[10:27] Alex Chen: None. We'll get materials out and schedule the benchmark.
[10:31] Lina Park: Thanks everyone.
[10:33] Samir Patel: Thanks.
[10:34] Alex Chen: Thanks all — we'll follow up with the doc pack and proposed SOW draft.
[10:38] [Call ended]

Notes about transcript quality: occasional overlaps and missing words due to call recording; proper nouns (e.g., some product names) may be slightly off.
